body: IPO May 1997 at $18. Splits 2:1 (1998), 3:1 (1999), 2:1 (1999), 20:1 (2022) = 240x: IPO ≈ $0.075 on today's basis. Dot-com peak Dec 1999 ~$107 nominal (~$4.4 adj) -> Sept 2001 ~$5.5 (~$0.28 adj): -94%. July 2021 peak ~$3,770 pre-2022-split (~$188): ~2,500x from IPO; ~670x from the 2001 low [split math mine]. Split: EPS was near-zero/negative for years by design; the driver was operating cash flow and later AWS profits; P/E is not meaningful. EARLY SIGNAL visible 1997-2002: the 1997 shareholder letter ('It's all about the long term', optimise for FCF per share, not GAAP EPS), negative working-capital cycle (paid by customers before paying suppliers), and customer counts compounding; Prime (2005) and AWS (2006) were later hidden segments — AWS was first broken out only in 2015, revealing a highly profitable cloud business. Who caught it: Bill Miller (Legg Mason) bought at the IPO, re-entered ~$88 pre-split in the late 1990s, and doubled down near ~$6 in 2001 after a -93% fall, reasoning the book business generated FCF with little inventory risk (247wallst); Nick Sleep/Qais Zakaria (Nomad, from ~2005) [unverified]. Ended/stalled: 2021 peak then -56% in 2022 (see case_study:amazon-drawdown). LESSON: the right metric can differ from EPS (FCF/share, unit economics); a founder willing to reinvest at scale and a hidden segment (AWS) can deliver 1,000x+, but only to holders who survive a -94% drawdown.

data.lesson: right metric + founder reinvestment + hidden segment; survive -94%

title: Amazon 1997-2021: ~2,500x via FCF per share, through a -94% crash
